title: Right-answer or open?

job.text: Five steps of a weekly report are listed below. For each one, decide who should own it: hand it to a tool if it has exactly one right answer, or leave it to the AI if it's a judgment call. Turn a chip on to route that step to a tool; leave it off to keep it with the AI.

naivePrompt: Do all five of these for me.
basePrompt: Do all five of these for me.

text.plain: Route the revenue total to a tool — it has exactly one right answer.
text.tech: Mark step 1 (revenue total) deterministic: true and attach a sum tool.

text.plain: Route the overdue-invoice count to a tool — it has exactly one right answer.
text.tech: Mark step 3 (invoice count) deterministic: true and attach a count tool.

text.plain: Route today's date to a tool — a lookup has exactly one right answer.
text.tech: Mark step 5 (today's date) deterministic: true and attach a date lookup.

text.plain: Route the friendly subject line to a tool — but it has no single right answer.
text.tech: Mark step 2 (subject line) deterministic: true — but it is open-ended.

text.plain: Route the suggested discount to a tool — but it's a judgment call, not a calculation.
text.tech: Mark step 4 (discount) deterministic: true — but it is a judgment call.

rules.claim: A tool was asked to write the subject line / pick the discount — and it couldn't.
rules.feedback: Over-tooled. A friendly subject line and a discount have no single right answer — a calculator can't write them. Not every step needs a gate.
rules.lesson: Don't gate the open steps; it just slows you down.

output.source: a tool asked to do an open-ended step

rules.claim: Total, count and date → tools (exact). Subject line and discount → the AI.
rules.feedback: Right owner for each step. The three exact steps go to tools; the two judgment steps stay with the AI. That's the whole game — and it's how World 7 thinks about a whole workflow.
rules.lesson: Match the owner to whether the step has one right answer.

output.source: the right owner for each step

rules.claim: A right-answer step was left to the AI — the total, the count or the date came back wrong.
rules.feedback: You left a right-answer step to the guesser. The total, the invoice count and today's date each have exactly one correct value — those go to a tool, every time.
rules.lesson: A step with one right answer is never the AI's job.

output.source: right-answer steps left to the AI

hints.nudge: If two careful people did this step, would they get the exact same answer? If yes, it's a tool step.
hints.gap: The total and the invoice count are clearly tool steps — that leaves three. Which of those three is also exact?
hints.moves: Today's date is a lookup → a tool. The subject line and the discount are judgment → leave them to the AI.

whatYouDoDifferently.naive: "Do all five" → the exact ones come back wrong.
whatYouDoDifferently.rewrite: Send the total, count and date to tools; leave the subject line and discount to the AI.

template.plain: For each step, tell me: does it have exactly one right answer? If yes, write me a tool (formula or script) for it. If it's a judgment call, just do your best and say so.
template.tech: Split the task: for each step annotate deterministic true | false. Build a tool for every deterministic step; leave the rest to best-effort generation.

notes: ChatGPT: ask it to split the task into "needs a tool" versus "judgment" before doing any of it.
Copilot in Excel: the exact steps become formulas; the wording stays prose.
A chat AI that can't run code: get the formulas for the exact steps and run them yourself; trust its prose only for the open steps, and never accept "I checked, the total's right."
